opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, because a lot of what makes a system good isn't captured in whether any one function is correct. It's the accumulated wisdom about how to structure things: keep interfaces simple, design for failure, measure before you optimize, and have a rough sense of how expensive different operations are, like a memory reference versus a disk seek versus a cross-datacenter round trip. Experienced engineers carry that around in their heads, and it shapes thousands of small decisions.

Coding agents today are quite good at producing locally plausible code, but they don't always have that broader sense of taste or the "why" behind certain patterns. So if you give them well-written guides, whether general principles or the specific conventions of a codebase, you're giving them the context a senior engineer would give a new team member. How do we handle errors here? How do we write tests? What are the performance expectations? When should you add a new abstraction versus reuse an existing one?

The other piece is that guides become more valuable as agents work over longer horizons. If an agent is only writing a ten-line function, it doesn't matter much. If it's building something substantial over many steps, small inconsistencies compound, and a shared set of principles keeps the whole thing coherent. It's similar to how style guides and design reviews help large human teams. They let lots of people contribute to the same system without it turning into a mess.

And I think it goes both ways. Writing these guides forces us to be explicit about practices that were often just tribal knowledge. That's good for the agents, and it's honestly good for the humans too.

r001.rationale: The response says guides provide context about conventions and practices, but does not explain that developers can use them to clarify prompts about intended system behavior.

r002.rationale: It says agents can benefit from general principles as well as codebase conventions, but does not state that general guides avoid needing a custom guide for every situation.

r003.rationale: It mentions “design for failure,” but does not propose a compact repertoire of distributed-system failure-handling techniques or connect that to building more reliable distributed systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Jeff Dean: You know, it's interesting, because a lot of what's in those guides was written down for humans who have a very particular set of limitations. We forget things. We get tired. We don't read the whole codebase before making a change. So a lot of the advice is really about managing human attention: keep functions small, write good names, don't have side effects at a distance, document your invariants.

And it turns out most of that transfers remarkably well to coding agents, but for slightly different reasons. An agent has a context window instead of working memory, but the failure mode is similar. If the information it needs to make a change correctly is scattered across twelve files and some tribal knowledge in someone's head, the agent is going to make the same kinds of mistakes a new hire would make in their first week. Maybe faster, and with more confidence, which is not always a good combination.

So I think of the guides as doing two things. One is that they tell you how to structure the system so that local reasoning is sufficient. That's the big one. If an agent can look at a module and its tests and have everything it needs, it will do well. If it has to understand the whole distributed system to safely touch one RPC handler, it won't, and frankly neither would most of us.

The second thing is that the guides encode a lot of taste about tradeoffs that aren't visible in any one piece of code. Why you'd want to batch requests. Why you shouldn't put a retry loop at every layer, because then you get exponential retry amplification when something fails. Why you measure before you optimize. Those are lessons that cost real outages to learn, and an agent that has internalized them from the written guidance avoids relearning them in production.

Where I'd push a little is that the guides shouldn't just be ingested as text. The agent is good at following rules; what you want is for the rules to be checkable. So the best version of a style guide for an agent is one where as much as possible is a linter, a type check, a test, a benchmark that fails loudly. Then the written document is there for the "why," and the tooling is there for the "whether." Agents are quite good at iterating against a signal. They're less good at knowing when they've quietly violated a principle that nobody enforces.

And the last thing I'd say is that this goes both directions. We've found that writing things down for the agents forces teams to make explicit a lot of things that were implicit. Which is good hygiene for the humans too. The team ends up with a better guide than they had before, because now there's a reader who will take every sentence literally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses guides and making their rules checkable, but does not say they help developers clarify prompts about intended system behavior.

r002.rationale: It says much general guidance transfers to agents, but does not state that this avoids needing custom guides for each situation.

r003.rationale: It gives distributed-systems examples such as batching and retry amplification, but does not propose a compact repertoire of failure-handling techniques as a way to build more reliable distributed systems.

astra-6.text:
I think they can help by making some of the judgment that goes into software engineering explicit. Getting a function to pass a test is one part of the problem. You also want the system to have sensible interfaces, to be easy to change, and to behave reasonably when something fails.

A useful guide can encourage the agent to step back and ask: What are the requirements? What code already exists that I should reuse? What’s the simplest design that satisfies those requirements? And how am I going to verify that it works?

The tricky part is applying that advice in context. You don’t want every small change to turn into a major architectural exercise. So I’d view these guides as useful defaults, coupled with feedback from the actual codebase, tests, and measurements. The goal is to help the agent make better engineering decisions, not just produce more code.

r001.rationale: It discusses making engineering judgment explicit and asking about requirements, but does not say developers can use guides to make their prompts clearer about intended system behavior.

r002.rationale: It presents guides as useful general defaults for agents, with context-specific feedback, rather than requiring a custom guide for each situation.

r003.rationale: It mentions sensible failure behavior generally, but does not propose a compact repertoire of distributed-system failure-handling techniques for building more reliable distributed systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they can help in much the same way they help human engineers: by making the things you ought to think about explicit. Getting a piece of code to work is one part of building a system. You also want to think about how it behaves when something fails, whether you can test it, and whether someone else can understand and modify it later.

A useful guide can give an agent a framework for those decisions. What are the requirements? What scale do we actually need to support? Where should the interfaces be? What evidence would convince us that this change is correct? And then the agent needs to connect that guidance to the particular codebase, rather than mechanically applying every best practice everywhere.

I think the feedback loop is really important, too. You want the agent to make a change, run tests, look at the results, and revise its approach. The guide helps it ask better questions, but actually checking what it built is what closes the loop.
